An L4 Planning Agent and an L1 LLM Workflow use the same model; the only difference is whether the model has the authority to decide the next step. This explains why swapping in a stronger model neither turns a Workflow into an Agent nor makes an out-of-control Agent reliable—the bottleneck is not the intelligence density inside nodes, but the control topology between them. To determine which level a system sits at, don't look at the framework or prompt depth; instead ask: if the model produces an unexpected but reasonable output order, does the system follow it or reject it? The steps that are followed constitute the true autonomous zone, and they define the direction of future engineering investment: the larger the autonomous zone, the more constraints, budgets, and audits are needed.

Among the three, reliability is the most easily underestimated: Workflow failures are explicit, localizable, and replayable, while Agent failures often manifest as "every step makes sense, but the whole trajectory goes off track," and no amount of retrying can fix it—only loop caps, whitelists, and checkpoints can keep the drift radius small. So the real cost question is: is the adaptability you buy back worth the premium? Most production incidents are not caused by choosing the wrong level, but by choosing a high level while doing capacity planning and SLA commitments under low-level assumptions.
y78fku:214: The continuous spectrum answers "how much authority to grant," while harness engineering answers "what will catch things once authority is granted." The higher the autonomy level, the heavier the harness responsibility—loop caps, tool whitelists, permission tiers, state persistence, human approval points, and budget circuit breakers are all essentially engineering means to re-structure part of the model's freedom. This also explains why engineered Agents converge into Agentic Workflows: not because they aren't intelligent enough, but because production systems require them to be budgetable, auditable, and rollback-able. Agentic Workflow is the steady-state of the enterprise-grade form.
